title: Contact-Governed Macroscopic Signatures of Strain-Induced Valley Sorting in MoS$_2$ Field-Effect Transistors
abstract: Strain engineering is a leading route to control valley-selective transport in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides. Whether this quantum effect survives inside a fully contacted device remains an open question. Quantum transport models capture the underlying valley deflection but are limited to isolated nanoscale fragments, leaving it unclear if a full device registers strain-induced valley sorting in the bulk, at the contacts, or at all. Here, the quantum valley-deflection tensor of strained monolayer MoS$_2$ is embedded directly into a macroscopic Poisson-drift-diffusion model, extending this physics to a complete, contact-inclusive device. Applying this framework to a 300~nm monolayer MoS$_2$ transistor with a 3~nm HfO$_2$ gate dielectric at 77~K, under a localized 6.14~T pseudo-magnetic strain field, shows the resulting 63.6\% suppression of the ON-state current is not a bulk property. It is set almost entirely by the source and drain metal-semiconductor interfaces. The full suppression is reproduced when only the 15~nm contact regions are strained and nearly vanishes when the channel interior alone is strained, identifying the metal contact as the dominant site of strain-induced valley physics. Observing it requires tunneling-transparent, degenerately-doped contacts, since classical Ohmic barriers overwhelm the topological signal. A transmission-line analysis reduces this behavior to a single valley-topological contact resistance ($R_{c,V}$) and a predictive inverse-length scaling law. This framework applies to any strain-engineered 2D-material heterostructure and can be tested with standard multi-length contact structures. Ultimately, these results identify the metal-semiconductor interface as the decisive location for engineering and detecting valley-selective transport in real 2D-material devices.
summary: This work addresses the challenge of observing quantum valley effects in real, macroscopic 2D-material transistors. By embedding quantum valley physics into a macroscopic drift-diffusion model, the authors demonstrate that the measurable signature of strain-induced valley sorting is overwhelmingly determined by the metal-semiconductor contacts, not the bulk channel. This identifies the contact interface as the critical engineering point for valley-selective transport.
main_problem: The core problem is determining if the quantum effect of strain-induced valley sorting, observed in isolated nanoscale fragments, survives and manifests macroscopically in a fully contacted 2D-material transistor.
main_result: The study concludes that the strain-induced valley physics is not a bulk channel property but is instead dominated by the metal-semiconductor source and drain contacts.
method: The authors developed a novel framework by embedding the quantum valley-deflection tensor into a macroscopic Poisson-drift-diffusion model, bridging quantum and classical transport descriptions.
model_or_system: The system is a monolayer MoS2 Field-Effect Transistor (FET) subjected to a localized pseudo-magnetic strain field. The physics is modeled using a two-band massive Dirac Hamiltonian and extended via a macroscopic transport model.
key_observables: Valley Topological Magnetoresistance (VTMR), measured as a percentage suppression of the ON-state current, and the derived valley-topological contact resistance ($R_{c,V}$).
important_parameters: Transistor length (300 nm), gate dielectric (3 nm HfO2), temperature (77 K), and localized strain field strength (6.14 T pseudo-magnetic field).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of tunneling-transparent, degenerately-doped contacts to prevent classical Ohmic barriers from overwhelming the topological signal.
figures_summary: Not specified (The notes describe the results derived from simulations rather than describing figure content).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the quantum Hamiltonian under strain, then developing a macroscopic transport model to incorporate this quantum effect into a full device structure, and finally applying this model to show that the measured signal originates entirely from the contacts.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state electronics, the methodology of bridging quantum Hamiltonian physics (valley deflection) into a continuum, macroscopic transport model is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems where boundary conditions dictate global behavior.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the high-κ monolayer MoS2 Valley-FET architecture. (a) Three-dimensional perspective illustrating the van der Waals heterostructure. From bottom to top, the piezoelectric actuator substrate provides the global strain platform, the back-gate electrode and 3 nm HfO2 gate dielec- tric form the electrostatic gate stack, and the hBN-buffered MoS2 monolayer channel carries the source and drain con- tacts. (b) Top-down quantum transport dynamics demon- strating the strain-induced pseudo-magnetic field separating K and K′ valley electrons to opposite transverse edges via the Valley Hall Effect.

FIG. 2. Spatial distribution of the normalized pseudo- magnetic gauge field and the corresponding macroscopic transport tensor. The right axis (red dashed line) traces the finite-element-derived Bz field, peaking at 6.14 T approxi- mately 15 nm inboard of each electrode rather than at the interface itself. The left axis (solid blue line) maps the result- ing mobility tensor µmod, demonstrating the symmetric struc- tural suppression from the intrinsic 3000 cm2/Vs acoustic- phonon limit down to a 698 cm2/Vs minimum, with partial recovery directly at the contact edge.

FIG. 3. Longitudinal macroscopic transport in the idealized Ohmic regime at 77 K. (a) The ID −VG transconductance curves demonstrating pure Drude-like linearity in the absence of an oxide barrier. (b) Macroscopic differential conductance (gd) extracted via linear regression confirming that the spatially varying topological strain induces a continuous suppression of the intrinsic sheet conductance from 579 mS/µm to 381 mS/µm.

FIG. 4. Steady-state transport characteristics of the fully gated High-κ MoS2 Valley-FET at 77 K. (a) Subthreshold electrostat- ics demonstrating consistent overlap and a similar subthreshold swing (∼102 mV/dec), indicating the strain tensor preserves gate integrity and OFF-state limits. (b) Linear ON-state transconductance revealing the macroscopic divergence between the control channel and the topological channel under high carrier density. (c) The Macroscopic Current Suppression mapping the percentage drop, which stabilizes into a 63.6% plateau as the transistor enters the deep inversion drift regime.

FIG. 5. Strain profile sensitivity analysis demonstrating the structural dominance of the source injection bottleneck at 77 K. (a) Spatial distributions of the pseudo-magnetic gauge field Bz across the 300 nm channel. The physically mandated contact-peaked Gaussian profile is compared against two extreme theoretical bounding conditions, a uniform 6.14 T field and a center-peaked field. (b) The corresponding macroscopic transfer characteristics. The uniform profile yields a larger ON-state suppression than the contact-peaked baseline (76.7% vs. 63.6%), indicating that bulk-channel strain contributes measurably to the total suppression rather than adding only negligible series resistance....
